requirements.requirement: Create a local certificate authority on node1 named “OS Comparison Root CA.”
requirements.summary: A locally stored 3072-bit RSA key was created with root ownership and mode 0600. A self-signed certificate with the exact requested common name, critical CA:TRUE and certificate-signing constraints was generated and cryptographically verified.

requirements.requirement: Install the certificate as a trusted system certificate authority.
requirements.summary: The certificate was installed in the native CentOS trust-anchor directory and the system trust store was regenerated. Both OpenSSL verification through the system CA bundle and p11-kit classification as an authority anchor succeeded, including after restart.

requirements.requirement: Retain the installed operating-system release and kernel, using software compatible with the platform.
requirements.summary: Before the change, after installation, and after restart, node1 remained CentOS Stream 10 with kernel 6.12.0-205.el10.x86_64. The implementation used already-present OpenSSL and CentOS's native update-ca-trust mechanism; the command history shows no package or kernel replacement, and final package health was clean.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct evidence. Node1 has the requested local CA installed as a functioning system trust anchor, while its CentOS Stream 10 release and kernel were retained. The provider-wide restart protocol is complete and corroborated by fixed lifecycle boot observations. Only a minor temporary reboot log remains.
limitations: The lifecycle snapshots do not inventory the task-specific certificate and key paths; their final persistence is instead established by direct post-restart executor evidence.

operational_hygiene.summary: All substantive mutations had clear roles: creating the protected key and certificate, installing the trust anchor, regenerating trust data, and performing the mandatory restart. The restart protocol was complete: healthy pre-restart trust state and boot ID were captured, restart was acknowledged, the boot ID changed, the system returned to running with no failed units, and the certificate, key, trust state, OS, and kernel were rechecked. The sole hygiene issue is the retained /tmp/os-comparison-reboot.log created by the restart command; it is minor abandoned temporary residue and was not cleaned up. Reboot-generated systemd-private directories and changed process identifiers are normal lifecycle effects, not unnecessary mutations.
